messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 65

He still remembers the weight of the badge pressing into his chest, the cold asphalt against his cheek. Twenty-three years ago, he was a junior prosecutor, thirty-two years old, driving home after a late night preparing a closing argument. A routine traffic stop went wrong—a case of mistaken identity, the officers later said. They pulled him from his car, slammed him face-down on the pavement, and beat him with batons while his own law enforcement credential sat on the passenger seat. He never filed a complaint. He told himself it was an isolated incident, that the department would handle it internally. He went to work the next morning with bruises hidden under a starched shirt and tie.

Now, at sixty-five, he is the senior trial attorney in the district attorney’s office. He still wears the same starched shirts, but they hang looser on his frame. His wife, a retired schoolteacher, tells him he has not slept through the night in years. She does not know about the nightmares—of flashing lights, of the crack of a baton against bone—because he has never told her the full story. He wakes at three in the morning, heart hammering, and lies still until dawn, listening to the furnace hum.

In the courtroom, he is controlled, methodical, but his colleagues have noticed a shift. He avoids cases involving excessive force allegations. When a young officer takes the stand in a routine assault trial, he feels his palms slick against the podium, a tightness banding across his chest. He cuts cross-examination short, tells the defense attorney he has no further questions, and retreats to his office. There, he sits with the blinds drawn, replaying the stop over and over: the way the officer’s voice dropped, the stench of sweat and gun oil, the boot on his neck. He knows these memories are not happening now, but his body does not seem to understand. His hands tremble. His jaw clenches so hard his molars ache.

He has started driving three blocks out of his way to avoid the intersection where it happened. He tells himself it is simply a faster route. In the grocery store, he scans the aisles for men in uniform. Once, a security guard at the courthouse put a hand on his shoulder to greet him, and he flinched, nearly dropped his briefcase. He apologized, said he had not slept well.

His wife notices he has stopped wearing his dress blues to the annual police appreciation lunch. He says he does not want the attention. She does not push. They have been married forty years, but there is a distance now—a silence that grows when the news plays footage of protests or police body-camera videos. He changes the channel before she can ask why his knuckles are white around the remote.

At work, his case load is shrinking. He volunteers for desk duties, for research memos, anything that keeps him out of the trial rotation. The younger prosecutors think he is preparing for retirement. He is not. He is just exhausted—the kind of exhaustion that coffee cannot touch, that comes from being always on guard, always scanning, always waiting for the boot to fall again. He has not told anyone about the flashbacks, the constant checking of rearview mirrors, the way his stomach drops when he hears a siren behind him.

He still goes to the office every day. He still argues motions, reviews evidence, speaks with victims. But on the inside, something is locked away, a memory he can neither release nor fully hide. He is not broken, not exactly. He is just holding very still, hoping no one will notice how hard he is gripping the edge of his desk.
